primaryText: I persuaded John for Bill to come.
comment: Rosenbaum's contrast with (14a) I hate for John to go: persuade takes no for-subject.

primaryText: I persuaded John for him to come.
comment: John and him are coindexed: not even a coreferent for-subject is possible under persuade.

primaryText: John arranged to meet at noon.
comment: Partial control: the collective meet needs a group subject including John.

primaryText: John managed to meet at noon.
John arranged for us/them to meet at noon.
comment: The source the Form Copy theory derives (48a) from by deleting for us/them (C1: 23-24, C2: fn. 118).

primaryText: John managed for us/them to meet at noon
comment: The paper prints no final period.

primaryText: Suzan could not attend, so she persuaded the chair to meet without her.
comment: Partial control (PRO indexed i+, the chair i) under a verb that takes no for-subject (15a,b).

primaryText: John wanted for us to meet without him.
context: Mary and I had a fight and we stopped talking. John, a good friend of both of us, is keen on getting us to be friends again. He insists that we meet but he feels it would be best if the meeting would be just between Mary and myself, without him.
comment: him is coindexed with John: the for-subject is free to exclude its antecedent.

primaryText: John wanted to meet without him.
context: Mary and I had a fight and we stopped talking. John, a good friend of both of us, is keen on getting us to be friends again. He insists that we meet but he feels it would be best if the meeting would be just between Mary and myself, without him.
comment: him j/*i: PRO (indexed i+) includes John, so him cannot refer to him (Condition B).

primaryText: I advised John for his team to meet without him.
context: John annoyed a number of people on his team at work, right before an important deadline. He asks for my advice on what they should do.
comment: him is coindexed with John. The page prints the pair as (57c), (57d); the prose calls them (57a), (57b).

primaryText: I advised John to meet without him.
context: John annoyed a number of people on his team at work, right before an important deadline. He asks for my advice on what they should do.
comment: him j/*i: PRO (indexed i+) includes John. The prose calls this example (57b).

primaryText: Only Peter arranged for his family/them to meet.
context: Peter, Jane and Adam are each making arrangements to have a meeting with their respective families.
comment: In the context the strict reading is true and the sloppy one false, so the sentence is possibly true.

context: Peter, Jane and Adam are each making arrangements to have a meeting with their respective families.
comment: The paper lists only the sloppy reading, false in the context: the sentence is necessarily false, so it has no strict reading.

primaryText: Only Peter arranged for his family/them to meet.
context: Peter, Jane and Adam are each making arrangements for Peter's family to meet.
comment: In the context the strict reading is false and the sloppy one true, so the sentence is possibly false. Footnote 18: the sloppy reading of them needs a paycheck construal.

context: Peter, Jane and Adam are each making arrangements for Peter's family to meet.
comment: The paper lists only the sloppy reading, true in the context: the sentence is necessarily true.
